content: The Rhizaria represent a significant lineage of protists. They exhibit a wide range of morphological diversity, but most members are amoeboid in nature, characterized by the presence of filose, reticulose, or microtubule-supported pseudopodia. A substantial number of Rhizaria produce intricate shells or skeletons, which contribute to the majority of protozoan fossils. Nearly all Rhizaria possess mitochondria with tubular cristae. The Rhizaria are divided into three primary groups: 1. Cercozoa: This group includes various amoebae and flagellates, typically possessing filose pseudopodia. They are commonly found in soil environments. 2. Foraminifera: These are amoeboids with reticulose pseudopodia and are predominantly found as marine benthic organisms. 3. Radiolaria: These amoeboids are characterized by axopods and are commonly found as marine plankton. Additional groups, such as Phytomyxea and Ascetosporea, may be included within the Cercozoa. Phytomyxea are plant parasites, while Ascetosporea are animal parasites. Another notable member is the peculiar amoeba Gromia. However, in some phylogenetic trees, these groups appear more closely related to the Foraminifera. The classification of Rhizaria as a cohesive group is primarily based on genetic similarities. Historically, they have been considered an extension of the Cercozoa. The term Rhizaria was introduced by Cavalier-Smith in 2002, who also included the centrohelids and Apusozoa within this expanded group. From an evolutionary perspective, Rhizaria belong to the Bikont clade, which also includes Archaeplastida, Chromalveolata, Excavata, and smaller unresolved groups like Apusozoa and Centrohelida. As bikonts, they are thought to have descended from a heterotrophic eukaryote with two flagella. It is hypothesized that Rhizaria share a closer evolutionary relationship with Excavata than with other groups, forming a clade sometimes referred to as Cabozoa. Historically, many Rhizarians were classified as animals due to their motility and heterotrophic nature. However, with the adoption of the five-kingdom system, which replaced the traditional animal-plant dichotomy, Rhizarians were reassigned to the kingdom Protista. Later, following Woese's introduction of the three-domain system and the recognition of the paraphyly of the kingdom Monera, taxonomists began to focus on the eukaryotic domain and the inherent paraphyly of Protista. After extensive debate, which continues to this day, Rhizaria have been recognized as a monophyletic group.
